ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A 1:1 Pulse Transformer (PT) is used to trigger the SCR in the below figure. The SCR is rated at $1.5 \mathrm{kV}, 250$ A with $I_L=250 \mathrm{~mA}, I_H=150 \mathrm{~mA}$, and $I_{G m a x}=150 \mathrm{~mA}$, $I_{\text {Gmin }}=100 \mathrm{~mA}$. The SCR is connected to an inductive load, where L $=150 \mathrm{mH}$ in series with a small resistance and the supply voltage is 200 V dc. The forward drops of all transistors/diodes and gate-cathode junction during ON state are 1.0 V
The minimum approximate volt-second rating of pulse transformer suitable for triggering the SCR should be : (volt-second rating is the maximum of product of the voltage and the width of the pulse that may applied)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left side of the figure is a pulse transformer labeled PT driven by a +10 V power supply and a lower switching transistor, and the transformer is 1:1; its secondary provides a trigger pulse to the gate-cathode circuit of the SCR on the right through a diode and resistor, and there is a clamping/bleeding branch; the SCR on the right is connected in series in a 200 V DC power supply and inductive load circuit, and the load contains an inductor L as well as a very small series resistor. Then reason: when the SCR is connected to an inductive load, the trigger pulse cannot be withdrawn too early, and must be maintained until the anode current rises to the latching current I_L. Take L=150 mH=0.15 H, I_L=250 mA=0.25 A, the supply is about 200 V, and the initial inductor current rises approximately linearly, so the required pulse width t≈L I_L / V = 0.15×0.25/200 = 1.875×10^-4 s = 187.5 µs. The PT primary is driven by a +10 V pulse; after subtracting the transistor on-state voltage drop of about 1 V, the primary voltage is about 9 V; even using 10 V as an approximation makes only a small difference. Therefore the minimum volt-second product is about 9×187.5≈1688 V·µs, or 10×187.5≈1875 V·µs. Taking about 2000 V·µs according to engineering approximation and margin, that is, about 2000 µ(V·s).

method.method_draft: First describe the image: identify the +10 V transistor-driven 1:1 PT, the secondary gate-drive path to the SCR, and the SCR connected to the 200 V dc inductive load. From the text take L = 150 mH, supply = 200 V, and latching current I_L = 250 mA. Since the SCR must remain gated until the load current reaches I_L, compute the required gate pulse width using the initial inductor current ramp t ≈ L I_L / V = 0.15 × 0.25 / 200 ≈ 187.5 µs. The primary of the 1:1 PT is driven by approximately the 10 V pulse, or about 9 V if the transistor on-drop is subtracted. Thus the required volt-second product is roughly 9–10 V × 188 µs ≈ 1.7–1.9 mV·s, rounded to the minimum approximate rating 2000 µV·s / 2000 V·µs.

The SCR is rated at $1.5 \mathrm{kV}, 250$ A with $I_L=250 \mathrm{~mA}, I_H=150 \mathrm{~mA}$, and $I_{G m a x}=150 \mathrm{~mA}$, $I_{\text {Gmin }}=100 \mathrm{~mA}$. The SCR is connected to an inductive load, where L $=150 \mathrm{mH}$ in series with a small resistance and the supply voltage is 200 V dc. The forward drops of all transistors/diodes and gate-cathode junction during ON state are 1.0 V. What is the minimum approximate volt-second rating of the pulse transformer suitable for triggering the SCR?
raw_record.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left side of the figure is a pulse transformer labeled PT driven by a +10 V power supply and a lower switching transistor, and the transformer is 1:1; its secondary provides a trigger pulse to the gate-cathode circuit of the SCR on the right through a diode and resistor, and there is a clamping/bleeding branch; the SCR on the right is connected in series in a 200 V DC power supply and inductive load circuit, and the load contains an inductor L as well as a very small series resistor. Then reason: when the SCR is connected to an inductive load, the trigger pulse cannot be withdrawn too early, and must be maintained until the anode current rises to the latching current I_L. Take L=150 mH=0.15 H, I_L=250 mA=0.25 A, the supply is about 200 V, and the initial inductor current rises approximately linearly, so the required pulse width t≈L I_L / V = 0.15×0.25/200 = 1.875×10^-4 s = 187.5 µs. The PT primary is driven by a +10 V pulse; after subtracting the transistor on-state voltage drop of about 1 V, the primary voltage is about 9 V; even using 10 V as an approximation makes only a small difference. Therefore the minimum volt-second product is about 9×187.5≈1688 V·µs, or 10×187.5≈1875 V·µs. Taking about 2000 V·µs according to engineering approximation and margin, that is, about 2000 µ(V·s).
